newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major worried about economic data leaks.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major worried about economic data leaks.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major expressed concern on Wednesday about the leak of official unemployment statistics for February, the third such incident in several months.
The Daily Mirror newspaper splashed news of a 68,200 fall in claimant unemployment across its Wednesday edition, hours before the Office for National Statistics officially confirmed the figures.
The mass-circulation tabloid also got hold of the unemployment figures in advance last month, although it got them wrong, apparently due to a printing error.
"Once might be an accident, twice might be coincidence, three times rather suggests it wasn't," Major said while campaigning for the May 1 general election.
The third occasion Major was referring to appeared to be the leak of last November's annual budget to the same newspaper. The Mirror did not publish anything in advance on that occasion.

Traders in the City of London, who react immediately to key statistics by adjusting the prices of shares, bonds and currencies, said leaks of sensitive data could be very unsettling for financial markets.
"You would have to trade on something like that," one dealer said. "It's a potential nightmare and the authorities have got to do something about it."

The Office for National Statistics (ONS), which puts out official economic data but had nothing to do with the budget, said a preliminary review of procedures within its labour market statistics division had been carried out.

"This has now been extended to a full review of security arrangements, including procedures for briefing other government departments and the control of confidential information within and outside the ONS," a spokesman said.
Dealers take a risk if they trade on leaks of figures.
Last month, the Mirror reported in advance that 57,800 people had been taken off the dole queues in January whereas the official figures showed 67,800 people found jobs.
"It certainly does not do the reputation of the ONS any good and may tarnish the City of London if it became endemic," a chief economist at a UK bank said.
"They have tightened up security over the last few years but it looks like they have got some more work to do."

The ONS releases official figures in regular "lock-ups" for financial news agency journalists, who are given press releases in a closed room up to 30 minutes in advance of their 0930 publication time.
Telephone and computer links with the outside world are severed during the embargo period.
But the statistics are also distributed to various government departments ahead of time, so leaks could spring from any number of places.
On the whole, Britain has a much better track record than many of its European counterparts in terms of keeping official statistics under wraps.
In Germany, for example, leaks of economic data are nothing new, with unemployment in particular often trickling out in advance.
Late in 1994, the German economics ministry was forced to deny it was the source of apparent leaks of industrial production and orders figures.
"It happens quite a lot on the continent. Cynics might suggest this is all part of our closer convergence with Europe," the chief economist said, tongue firmly in cheek.
